anchor: The Principle of Moments > Sorting Turning Effects by Direction > You must always check both the force direction and its position relative to your chosen point.
title: Classifying Moments by Turning Direction
action: Classify the turning direction of each force about pivot P.
prompt: A uniform horizontal bar is pivoted at its center P. For each of the following forces, determine whether it produces a clockwise, anticlockwise, or zero moment about P: (1) A downward force acting to the right of P; (2) A downward force acting to the left of P; (3) An upward force acting to the right of P; (4) A vertical force whose line of action passes directly through P.
options: 1: Clockwise, 2: Anticlockwise, 3: Anticlockwise, 4: Zero moment
1: Anticlockwise, 2: Clockwise, 3: Clockwise, 4: Zero moment
1: Clockwise, 2: Clockwise, 3: Anticlockwise, 4: Zero moment
1: Clockwise, 2: Anticlockwise, 3: Clockwise, 4: Clockwise

feedback.1: Clockwise, 2: Anticlockwise, 3: Antic: Correct. A downward force on the right turns the bar clockwise. A downward force on the left turns it anticlockwise. An upward force on the right lifts that side and turns it anticlockwise. A force acting through P has zero perpendicular distance, so its moment is zero.
feedback.1: Anticlockwise, 2: Clockwise, 3: Clock: Incorrect. A downward force on the right pushes that side down, which corresponds to clockwise rotation, not anticlockwise.
feedback.1: Clockwise, 2: Clockwise, 3: Anticlock: Incorrect. A downward force on the left turns the bar anticlockwise, not clockwise. The position relative to the pivot reverses the turning direction.
feedback.1: Clockwise, 2: Anticlockwise, 3: Clock: Incorrect. A force passing directly through the pivot has a perpendicular distance of zero, producing zero moment rather than a clockwise moment.

anchor: The Principle of Moments > The Principle of Moments and Rotational Balance > Rotational balance always demands one common reference point.
title: Assembling the Principle of Moments
action: Select the option that gives the exact and complete statement of the principle of moments.
prompt: Which statement correctly and completely states the principle of moments according to the Cambridge syllabus standard?
options: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point
when forces act on a body, the total clockwise moment equals the total anticlockwise moment
for a body in rotational equilibrium, the clockwise moments about one pivot equal the anticlockwise moments about another pivot
for a stationary body, the sum of all upward forces equals the sum of all downward forces
answer: for a body in rotational equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point equals the sum of anticlockwise moments about the same point

feedback.for a body in rotational equilibrium, th: Correct. This is the exact Cambridge definition. It explicitly requires both rotational equilibrium and that moments are evaluated about the same point.
feedback.when forces act on a body, the total clo: Incorrect. This omits two essential marking criteria: the condition of rotational equilibrium and the requirement that moments must be taken about the same point.
feedback.for a body in rotational equilibrium, th: Incorrect. Clockwise and anticlockwise moments must be evaluated about the same point, never about different pivots.
feedback.for a stationary body, the sum of all up: Incorrect. This describes translational equilibrium of vertical forces, not the principle of moments.

anchor: The Principle of Moments > Formulating and Solving Moment Balance Equations > Group all clockwise moments on one side of the equation.
title: Setting Up Rotational Balance Equations
action: Select the correct rotational balance equation for the given pivoted beam.
prompt: A light horizontal rod is pivoted at point P. A 20 N downward force acts 0.30 m to the left of P. On the right of P, a 15 N downward force acts 0.20 m from P and an unknown downward force F acts 0.50 m from P. If the rod is in rotational equilibrium, which equation correctly represents the principle of moments about P?

feedback.20 \u00d7 0.30 = (15 \u00d7 0.20) + (F \: Correct. The 20 N force on the left turns the rod anticlockwise. The 15 N and F forces on the right turn the rod clockwise. Equating anticlockwise and clockwise moments gives 20 × 0.30 = (15 × 0.20) + (F × 0.50).
feedback.(20 \u00d7 0.30) + (15 \u00d7 0.20) = F: Incorrect. The 15 N force acts to the right of the pivot and turns the bar clockwise, so it belongs on the same side as F, not with the anticlockwise 20 N force.
feedback.20 \u00d7 0.50 = (15 \u00d7 0.20) + (F \: Incorrect. Distances have been swapped between forces. Each force must strictly be multiplied by its own perpendicular distance from P.
feedback.20 + 15 + F = 0: Incorrect. This attempts to sum force magnitudes rather than moments. Rotational balance requires balancing turning effects (force multiplied by distance), not force magnitudes.

anchor: The Principle of Moments > Strategic Pivot Selection to Eliminate Unknown Forces > When the line of action of a force passes through the chosen reference point, its perpendicular distance is zero.
title: Choosing a Strategic Pivot Point
action: Select the most effective reference point to find the unknown cable tension in a single equation.
prompt: A horizontal beam AB is attached to a vertical wall by a hinge at A. Its weight acts downwards at midpoint C. A heavy crate rests at point D near the free end B. An angled support cable connects end B to the wall above. You need to calculate the tension in the cable without first finding the wall reaction force at hinge A. About which point should you take moments?
options: Hinge A, because the line of action of the unknown wall reaction passes through A and has zero moment.
Midpoint C, because the weight of the beam has zero moment about its own centre of gravity.
Point D, because the heavy crate has zero moment about its contact point.
End B, because the cable tension has zero moment about its attachment point.
answer: Hinge A, because the line of action of the unknown wall reaction passes through A and has zero moment.

feedback.Hinge A, because the line of action of t: Correct. Taking moments about hinge A sets the perpendicular distance of the unknown hinge force to zero, eliminating it from the moment equation in one step.
feedback.Midpoint C, because the weight of the be: Incorrect. Taking moments about C removes the known beam weight, but leaves both the unknown hinge reaction and the unknown cable tension in the equation.
feedback.Point D, because the heavy crate has zer: Incorrect. Taking moments about D leaves two simultaneous unknown forces (hinge reaction and cable tension) in the equation.
feedback.End B, because the cable tension has zer: Incorrect. Taking moments about B eliminates the very quantity (cable tension) that you want to calculate.

anchor: The Principle of Moments > Reaction Forces and the Tipping Threshold > The contact reaction force at that far support drops to exactly zero.
title: Deducing Conditions at the Tipping Threshold
action: Identify what happens to the support forces when a beam is on the verge of tipping.
prompt: A uniform plank rests horizontally across two sawhorses, support 1 on the left and support 2 on the right. A worker walks past support 2 towards the far right overhang. As the worker reaches the critical position where the plank is just on the verge of tipping, what happens to the support forces R1 and R2?
options: R1 becomes zero because the plank loses contact with support 1, while R2 supports the entire downward weight.
R2 becomes zero because the plank tips over support 2, while R1 supports the entire downward weight.
Both R1 and R2 remain equal and non-zero until after the plank has fallen.
R1 doubles while R2 drops to half of its original value.
answer: R1 becomes zero because the plank loses contact with support 1, while R2 supports the entire downward weight.

feedback.R1 becomes zero because the plank loses: Correct. As the worker walks past support 2, the clockwise moment tilts the plank about support 2, lifting it off support 1. At the tipping point, contact with support 1 is lost, so R1 = 0.
feedback.R2 becomes zero because the plank tips o: Incorrect. Support 2 is the pivot point about which the plank tilts; the plank maintains contact with support 2 while lifting off support 1.
feedback.Both R1 and R2 remain equal and non-zero: Incorrect. The load distribution shifts continuously as the worker moves. Contact force R1 steadily decreases until it reaches zero at the tipping threshold.
feedback.R1 doubles while R2 drops to half of its: Incorrect. Shifting the load to the right decreases the reaction force at the left support R1, driving it to zero, not doubling it.
